questions.q: Which bony landmark marks the junction between the manubrium and body of the sternum at approximately the level of the second costal cartilage and the T4/T5 intervertebral disc?
questions.explain: The sternal angle is a palpable transverse ridge where the manubrium meets the sternal body, serving as a key surface landmark for counting ribs (starting at the second costal cartilage), locating the aortic arch/bifurcation of trachea, and marking the T4/T5 disc plane.

open.q: What palpable ridge marks the junction of the manubrium and sternal body at the level of the second costal cartilage?

questions.q: Ribs 1 through 7 are classified as true (vertebrosternal) ribs because of how they attach anteriorly?
options: They articulate with the sternum only via the seventh costal cartilage
Each connects directly to the sternum via its own costal cartilage
They end freely within the anterior abdominal wall musculature
questions.explain: True ribs (ribs 1 to 7) each have their own costal cartilage that articulates directly with the sternum. False ribs (8 to 10) join the costal cartilage above, while floating ribs (11 and 12) have no anterior attachment to the sternum.

open.q: How do true ribs (ribs 1 to 7) attach anteriorly to the sternum?
accept: each attaches directly to the sternum via its own costal cartilage
each has its own costal cartilage joining the sternum directly
direct attachment to the sternum by their own costal cartilages

questions.q: Which ribs are classified as floating (vertebral) ribs because their cartilaginous tips end freely in the posterior abdominal wall musculature without reaching the sternum?
questions.explain: Ribs 11 and 12 are floating ribs whose small cartilaginous tips end freely in the musculature of the posterior abdominal wall rather than articulating with the sternum or another rib cartilage.

open.q: Which two ribs are floating ribs whose tips end freely in musculature?

questions.q: Along which part of a typical rib does the costal groove run to protect the intercostal vein, artery, and nerve?
options: Inferior internal aspect of the shaft
questions.explain: The costal groove lies along the inferior internal margin of a typical rib shaft, sheltering the intercostal vein (most superior), intercostal artery, and intercostal nerve (most inferior, VAN from above downward).

open.q: Along which border/aspect of a typical rib does the costal groove run?
accept: inferior internal aspect of the shaft
lower inner border of the rib

questions.q: Why should a thoracentesis or intercostal chest tube insertion pass just above the superior border of the lower rib in an intercostal space?
options: To avoid the main intercostal neurovascular bundle beneath the rib above
There are no muscles above a rib
The diaphragm attaches only to rib superior borders
questions.explain: The main intercostal vein, artery, and nerve run in the costal groove along the inferior margin of the rib above, so inserting just superior to the lower rib avoids the main neurovascular bundle (though collateral branches can exist).

open.q: Why is a needle or chest tube inserted just above the superior border of a rib during intercostal procedures?
accept: to avoid the main neurovascular bundle in the costal groove of the rib above
to stay clear of the intercostal vessels and nerve below the upper rib
to avoid injuring the intercostal vein, artery, and nerve

questions.q: Which intercostal muscles run inferoanteriorly from the rib above to the rib below and assist inspiration by elevating the ribs?
questions.explain: External intercostal muscles have fibers directed inferoanteriorly (hands in pockets anteriorly) and extend from tubercles posteriorly to near the costochondral junctions anteriorly, elevating ribs during quiet/active inspiration.

open.q: Which intercostal muscles have fibers running inferoanteriorly and help elevate the ribs during inspiration?

questions.q: How does the pump-handle movement of the ribs increase the anteroposterior diameter of the thoracic cavity during inspiration?
options: Ribs rotate around a vertical sternal axis
Anterior rib elevation moves the sternum forward and up, increasing AP diameter
Costal cartilages shorten and pull the sternum back
questions.explain: Because the anterior ends of the ribs lie lower than their posterior vertebral attachments, elevating the rib bodies causes the sternum and anterior rib ends to move forward and upward (pump-handle motion), expanding anteroposterior thoracic dimension.

open.q: How does pump-handle motion of the ribs expand the anteroposterior diameter of the thorax?
accept: anterior ends of the ribs and sternum rise and move forward
elevation of rib shafts pushes the anterior ends and sternum anteriorly
raising the anterior rib ends increases anteroposterior chest depth

questions.q: At which vertebral level does the aortic hiatus pass through the diaphragm?
questions.explain: Using the classic levels: caval opening is at T8 (IVC), esophageal hiatus is at T10 (esophagus and vagal trunks), and aortic hiatus is at T12 (aorta, thoracic duct, and often azygos vein).

open.q: At which vertebral level does the aortic hiatus pass through the diaphragm?

questions.q: Which nerve provides the primary motor innervation to the diaphragm?
questions.explain: The phrenic nerve arises from cervical spinal segments C3, C4, and C5 (C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive), descending through the thorax to supply motor fibers to the diaphragm and sensory fibers to its central tendon and mediastinal/diaphragmatic pleura.

open.q: Which nerve provides motor supply to the diaphragm?

questions.q: A patient has irritation of the diaphragmatic pleura or peritoneum beneath the central tendon of the diaphragm and feels referred pain over the ipsilateral shoulder tip. Which nerve pathway explains this referred pain?
options: Phrenic afferents (C3–C5) share segments with shoulder sensation
questions.explain: Sensory fibers from the central diaphragm travel in the phrenic nerve (C3 to C5) to the same cervical cord levels that receive cutaneous input from the shoulder via supraclavicular nerves (C3 to C4), producing referred shoulder-tip pain.

open.q: Which nerve explains referred pain to the shoulder tip from irritation of the central diaphragm?
accept: c3 to c5 phrenic and supraclavicular pathway

questions.q: Which layer of the pleura adheres directly to the surface of the lung and dips into its fissures?
questions.explain: The visceral (pulmonary) pleura covers the lung surfaces and lines the interlobar fissures, whereas the parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall, mediastinum, and diaphragm.

open.q: Which pleural layer closely covers the lung surfaces and enters its fissures?

questions.q: Why does the inferior margin of the parietal pleura extend lower than the inferior border of the lung (for example, to the 10th rib at the midaxillary line)?
options: It forms a recess into which the lung expands on deep inspiration
Parietal pleura attaches to the xiphoid
questions.explain: Because the inferior border of the lung sits higher than the inferior reflection of parietal pleura, a potential space called the costodiaphragmatic recess is formed, allowing the lower lung margin to descend during deep inspiration.

open.q: What space is created because the parietal pleura extends lower than the inferior border of the lung?

questions.q: How many lobes and fissures does the right lung typically possess?
options: Two lobes and one oblique fissure
Three lobes and one horizontal fissure only
Three lobes divided by oblique and horizontal fissures
questions.explain: The right lung has three lobes—superior, middle, and inferior—separated by an oblique fissure and a horizontal fissure. The left lung has two lobes (superior and inferior) separated by an oblique fissure.

open.q: How many lobes and fissures does the right lung typically have?
accept: 3 lobes with oblique and horizontal fissures
three lobes, oblique and horizontal fissures

questions.q: Which structural feature on the medial surface of the left lung accommodates the apex and left side of the heart?
questions.explain: The anterior border of the left lung presents a prominent cardiac notch (with a tongue-like lingula below it) where the left heart borders approach the thoracic wall.

open.q: What indentation on the anterior border of the left lung accommodates the heart?

questions.q: Why are inhaled foreign bodies more likely to enter the right main bronchus than the left main bronchus?
options: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical
The right bronchus is narrower and more horizontal
The carina directs all particles left
questions.explain: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and takes a steeper, more vertical path from the trachea than the narrower, longer, more horizontal left main bronchus, making aspirated objects more common on the right.

open.q: Why are aspirated foreign bodies more likely to enter the right main bronchus than the left?
accept: it is wider, shorter, and more vertical
wider, shorter, and steeper alignment with the trachea

questions.q: A trauma patient has absent breath sounds, hyperresonance to percussion, and tracheal deviation away from the affected side with distended neck veins and hypotension. Which life-threatening condition is present?
questions.explain: A one-way air leak into the pleural space creates a tension pneumothorax, increasing intrapleural pressure, collapsing the ipsilateral lung, shifting the mediastinum/trachea contralaterally, and impairing venous return to the heart.

open.q: Which condition causes hyperresonance, absent breath sounds, contralateral tracheal shift, and hemodynamic compromise from trapped pleural air?

questions.q: What is a bronchopulmonary segment?
options: A subdivision of a lung lobe supplied by a secondary (lobar) bronchus and lobar pulmonary artery.
A subdivision of a lung lobe supplied by a segmental bronchus and a corresponding branch of the pulmonary artery.
A microscopic unit of lung parenchyma supplied by a terminal bronchiole and bounded by connective-tissue septa.
A region of lung supplied by a segmental bronchus but enclosed within its own separate pleural sac.
questions.explain: A bronchopulmonary segment is a distinct, roughly pyramidal subdivision of a lung lobe supplied by its own segmental (tertiary) bronchus and a corresponding segmental branch of the pulmonary artery. Its base faces the pleural surface and its apex points toward the hilum. Connective-tissue septa separate adjacent segments, while pulmonary veins usually run between them; this anatomical independence allows a segment to be removed surgically (segmentectomy) while preserving the rest of the lobe.

open.q: What is a bronchopulmonary segment?
accept: a discrete functional lung unit supplied by a tertiary bronchus and segmental artery
functional unit of a lung lobe supplied by a segmental bronchus
wedge-shaped lung unit supplied by a tertiary bronchus

questions.q: Which division of the mediastinum contains the heart within the pericardium?
questions.explain: The inferior mediastinum is divided into anterior, middle, and posterior parts relative to the pericardial sac; the middle mediastinum contains the pericardium, heart, ascending aorta, pulmonary trunk, and SVC termination.

open.q: Which division of the mediastinum houses the pericardium and heart?

questions.q: Which major structure passes through the superior mediastinum and arches over the root of the left lung and left main bronchus?
questions.explain: The aortic arch lies in the superior mediastinum, arching posteriorly and to the left above the left pulmonary hilum/bronchus as it continues as the thoracic aorta.

open.q: Which major vessel arches over the left main bronchus in the superior mediastinum?

questions.q: How does the course of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve differ from that of the right recurrent laryngeal nerve?
options: Left loops under right subclavian; right under aortic arch
Left loops under aortic arch; right under right subclavian
Neither nerve loops beneath a vessel
Both pass through the T8 caval opening
questions.explain: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks beneath the aortic arch (just lateral to the ligamentum arteriosum) and ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove, whereas the right recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the right subclavian artery.

open.q: Beneath which vessel does the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hook compared with the right?
accept: under the aortic arch while the right hooks under the right subclavian artery
aortic arch on the left and right subclavian artery on the right

questions.q: Which layer of the pericardium is a tough, inelastic outer sac that prevents sudden overdistension of the heart and blends inferiorly with the central tendon of the diaphragm?
questions.explain: The fibrous pericardium is the tough outer dense connective tissue sac of the pericardium, lined internally by the parietal serous pericardium. Together with the visceral serous layer (epicardium), they enclose the pericardial cavity.

open.q: Which tough outer layer of the pericardium resists acute overdistension of the heart?

questions.q: What is the clinical significance of the transverse pericardial sinus located behind the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk and anterior to the superior vena cava?
options: It permits clamping of the aorta and pulmonary trunk
It separates tricuspid valve from right atrium
questions.explain: The transverse pericardial sinus lies between the arterial outflow vessels (aorta and pulmonary trunk) anteriorly and the great veins/atria posteriorly, allowing surgical access to pass a finger or clamp around the aorta and pulmonary trunk.

open.q: How is the transverse pericardial sinus useful during cardiac surgery?
accept: it allows passing a clamp or ligature around the aorta and pulmonary trunk
surgeons can pass a finger or clamp behind the aorta and pulmonary trunk
isolating the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk

questions.q: Which chamber of the heart forms most of the sternocostal (anterior) surface of the heart?
questions.explain: The right ventricle makes up the largest portion of the anterior (sternocostal) surface of the heart, while the left ventricle forms most of the diaphragmatic (inferior) surface and the apex.

open.q: Which heart chamber forms most of the anterior (sternocostal) surface?

questions.q: Where is the apex of the normal adult heart typically located on the anterior chest wall?
options: Left 3rd intercostal space, anterior axillary line
Left 5th intercostal space, near the midclavicular line
questions.explain: The heart apex is formed by the inferolateral left ventricle and typically lies in the fifth left intercostal space (often about 7 to 9 cm from the midline or just medial to the midclavicular line in adults).

open.q: In which intercostal space is the normal adult cardiac apex typically located?

questions.q: Which valve guards the right atrioventricular orifice between the right atrium and right ventricle?
questions.explain: The tricuspid (right atrioventricular) valve has three cusps (anterior, septal, and posterior) attached via chordae tendineae to papillary muscles of the right ventricle.

open.q: Which valve lies between the right atrium and right ventricle?

questions.q: Why do chordae tendineae and papillary muscles prevent prolapse of the atrioventricular valves into the atria during ventricular systole?
options: They close semilunar valves in diastole
They tense chordae during systole, preventing AV valve prolapse
They pump coronary-sinus blood into ventricles
They fuse valve leaflets to the septum
questions.explain: As ventricular pressure rises during systole, papillary muscles contract and pull on the chordae tendineae, anchoring the atrioventricular valve cusps so they do not evert/prolapse back into the atria.

open.q: How do papillary muscles and chordae tendineae prevent atrioventricular valve prolapse during systole?
accept: they tense the cusps so rising ventricular pressure does not push them into the atria
papillary contraction pulls chordae tendineae to keep valve leaflets from everting
holding valve cusps taut during ventricular contraction

questions.q: From which sinuses do the right and left coronary arteries arise?
options: Aortic sinuses of the ascending aorta
questions.explain: The right and left coronary arteries arise from the right and left aortic sinuses of the ascending aorta just superior to the aortic valve cusps (the posterior non-coronary sinus gives rise to no coronary artery).

open.q: From which structures do the right and left coronary arteries originate?

questions.q: Which major branch of the left coronary artery runs down the anterior interventricular sulcus and supplies much of the anterior interventricular septum and anterior left ventricular wall?
questions.explain: The anterior interventricular artery (left anterior descending, LAD) courses along the anterior interventricular sulcus toward the apex, supplying the anterior left ventricle, right ventricle adjacent to the groove, and anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum.

open.q: Which branch of the left coronary artery runs in the anterior interventricular sulcus?

questions.q: A patient has an acute occlusion of the anterior interventricular (LAD) artery. Which region of the heart is most directly at risk of ischemia or infarction?
options: Anterior LV wall and anterior interventricular septum
questions.explain: Occlusion of the anterior interventricular (LAD) artery classically causes ischemia/infarction of the anterior wall of the left ventricle, the apex, and the anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum.

open.q: Which heart regions are primarily threatened by occlusion of the anterior interventricular artery?
accept: anterior left ventricular wall and anterior interventricular septum
anterior left ventricle and anterior septum
anterior wall of left ventricle and septum

questions.q: Where is the sinoatrial (SA) node, the normal pacemaker of the heart, typically located?
options: Upper right atrium near SVC opening
questions.explain: The sinoatrial (SA) node lies in the epicardial/myocardial wall of the upper right atrium near the entry of the superior vena cava and superior end of the crista terminalis.

open.q: Where in the heart is the sinoatrial (SA) node typically located?
accept: upper right atrium near the superior vena cava opening
right atrium near superior vena cava
upper right atrium at junction with superior vena cava

questions.q: Into which heart chamber does the coronary sinus—the main venous channel draining most of the heart wall—empty?
questions.explain: The coronary sinus runs in the posterior atrioventricular groove and empties deoxygenated cardiac venous blood into the right atrium between the inferior vena cava opening and the right atrioventricular orifice.

open.q: Into which chamber of the heart does the coronary sinus drain?

questions.q: Which vein ascends along the posterior thoracic wall to the right of the vertebral bodies and arches over the root of the right lung to join the superior vena cava?
questions.explain: The azygos vein drains posterior intercostal veins, bronchial/esophageal/pericardial veins, and the hemiazygos/accessory hemiazygos systems, arching over the right lung root at about T4 to empty into the superior vena cava.

open.q: Which longitudinal vein of the posterior thorax arches over the right lung root to enter the superior vena cava?

questions.q: Which pair of arteries arises directly from the internal thoracic (internal mammary) artery in each of the anterior intercostal spaces 1 through 6?
questions.explain: The internal thoracic artery descends behind the upper six costal cartilages and gives off anterior intercostal arteries to the anterior intercostal spaces 1 to 6, dividing inferiorly at the sixth intercostal space into musculophrenic and superior epigastric arteries.

open.q: Which arteries arise from the internal thoracic artery to supply the anterior intercostal spaces?

questions.q: Into which two terminal branches does the internal thoracic artery bifurcate at about the sixth intercostal space?
questions.explain: At approximately the sixth intercostal space, the internal thoracic artery divides into the musculophrenic artery (following the costal margin) and the superior epigastric artery (entering the rectus sheath).

open.q: What are the two terminal branches of the internal thoracic artery?

questions.q: How does the esophagus change its anatomical relationship to the aorta as it descends through the posterior mediastinum?
options: It begins anterior/right of the aorta and moves leftward toward the oesophageal hiatus
It stays posterior to the aorta throughout
It crosses the diaphragm at T8 with the IVC
It lies wholly inside the pericardium
questions.explain: In the posterior mediastinum, the esophagus initially lies to the right and anterior to the descending thoracic aorta, then inclines anteriorly and to the left so it lies anterior to the lower aorta before passing through the T10 esophageal hiatus.

open.q: How does the esophagus shift position relative to the descending thoracic aorta in the posterior mediastinum?
accept: from right/anterior to more anterior and left of the lower thoracic aorta
it moves anteriorly and to the left relative to the descending aorta
from right of the aorta to anterior to the lower aorta

questions.q: A patient with severe coarctation of the aorta has increased pressure proximal to the narrowing and develops enlarged collateral arteries along the posterior intercostal spaces that groove the inferior borders of ribs on chest radiograph. Which radiological sign is this?
questions.explain: Collateral blood flow from internal thoracic/subscapular/transverse cervical pathways into posterior intercostal arteries increases flow and pressure in these vessels, causing pressure erosion or notching along the inferior rib margins (rib notching).

open.q: What radiographic finding on the ribs can result from dilated collateral posterior intercostal arteries in aortic coarctation?

questions.q: Where is the intercostobrachial nerve (typically lateral cutaneous branch of T2) distributed?
options: Axillary floor and proximal medial arm
questions.explain: The intercostobrachial nerve is the lateral cutaneous branch of the second intercostal nerve (T2) that crosses the axilla to supply skin of the axillary floor and medial side of the upper arm, explaining why cardiac pain can refer to the medial arm.

open.q: Which cutaneous territory is supplied by the intercostobrachial nerve?
accept: axilla and medial aspect of the upper arm
floor of the axilla and medial upper arm

questions.q: Why does cardiac ischemic pain sometimes radiate to the medial aspect of the left arm and forearm?
options: Left phrenic nerve directly innervates ulnar nerve
Cardiac afferents enter T1–T4/5, overlapping with medial-arm somatic input
Left coronary artery continues as radial artery
Myocardium receives brachial plexus motor fibres
questions.explain: Visceral sensory fibers from the heart travel via sympathetic pathways to upper thoracic spinal cord segments (T1 to T4/T5), sharing dorsal horn neurons with somatic afferents from the medial arm/axilla (T1 to T2 via intercostobrachial/medial brachial cutaneous pathways).

open.q: Why can cardiac pain refer to the medial left arm and forearm?
accept: shared upper thoracic spinal cord segments between cardiac afferents and medial arm sensory fibers
convergence of cardiac sympathetic afferents and t1-t2 medial arm somatic afferents
overlapping upper thoracic spinal cord segments

questions.q: Which structures form the root (hilum) of each lung where bronchi, vessels, nerves, and lymphatics enter or leave?
options: Main bronchus, pulmonary vessels, bronchial vessels, nerves and lymphatics
Phrenic nerve and thoracic duct only
Coronary sinus and great cardiac vein
questions.explain: The root of the lung consists of the main bronchus, pulmonary artery, two pulmonary veins, bronchial arteries and veins, pulmonary nerve plexus, and bronchopulmonary lymph nodes enclosed by a cuff of pleura.

open.q: What main structures make up the root of the lung?
accept: bronchus, pulmonary artery, pulmonary veins, bronchial vessels, nerves, and lymphatics
main bronchus, pulmonary artery, and pulmonary veins with bronchial vessels, nerves, and lymphatics

questions.q: In the right lung root, how is the pulmonary artery positioned relative to the bronchi?
options: It lies inferior and anterior to the right eparterial bronchus
It passes below the diaphragm before entering the lung
questions.explain: In the right lung root, the superior lobar (eparterial) bronchus lies superior to the right pulmonary artery, while the right pulmonary artery lies anterior and inferior to it and anterior to the continuation of the bronchus.

open.q: How does the right pulmonary artery relate to the superior lobar bronchus at the right hilum?
accept: it lies inferior and anterior to the superior lobar bronchus
inferior and anterior to the eparterial bronchus
below and in front of the superior lobar bronchus

questions.q: Which bone articulates with the medial end of the clavicle and the first seven costal cartilages?
questions.explain: The sternum—comprising the manubrium, body, and xiphoid process—articulates with the clavicles at the clavicular notches of the manubrium and receives costal cartilages 1 through 7 along its lateral borders.

open.q: Which bone articulates with the medial end of the clavicle and costal cartilages 1 to 7?

questions.q: At which vertebral level does the caval opening (foramen venae cavae) pierce the central tendon of the diaphragm?
questions.explain: The caval opening lies in the central tendon of the diaphragm at approximately the T8 vertebral level and transmits the inferior vena cava and right phrenic nerve branches.

open.q: At which vertebral level does the inferior vena cava pass through the diaphragm?

questions.q: What is the role of pulmonary surfactant produced by type II alveolar pneumocytes?
options: It raises surface tension and collapses alveoli
It lowers surface tension and reduces alveolar collapse
It carries oxygen from pulmonary veins
questions.explain: Pulmonary surfactant reduces surface tension at the alveolar air-liquid interface, preventing alveolar collapse (atelectasis) at low lung volumes and making inflation easier (higher compliance).

open.q: How does pulmonary surfactant affect surface tension and stability in the alveoli?
accept: it lowers surface tension and helps prevent alveolar collapse
reduces surface tension and increases lung compliance
decreases surface tension to keep alveoli open

questions.q: A patient develops fluid accumulation in the pericardial space after pericarditis, causing elevated jugular venous pressure, muffled heart sounds, and hypotension. Which triad is described?
questions.explain: Beck triad consists of hypotension, distended neck veins (elevated JVP), and muffled/distant heart sounds, classic for acute cardiac tamponade when pericardial fluid compresses the heart chambers.

open.q: What clinical triad of hypotension, elevated JVP, and muffled heart sounds is associated with cardiac tamponade?

questions.q: Which structure forms the muscular interventricular septum that separates the right and left ventricles?
options: A muscular partition with a smaller superior membranous part
questions.explain: The interventricular septum is mostly a thick muscular wall between the right and left ventricles, with a smaller superior membranous portion near the right fibrous trigone and tricuspid septal leaflet.

open.q: What is the main structural composition of the interventricular septum of the heart?
accept: a thick muscular septum with a smaller superior membranous portion
mostly muscular tissue with a membranous part superiorly
muscular wall with a small membranous part

questions.q: Which artery gives rise to the posterior interventricular (posterior descending) artery in a right-dominant heart?
questions.explain: In right coronary dominance (the most common pattern), the right coronary artery gives off the posterior interventricular (descending) artery in the posterior interventricular sulcus to supply the posterior septum and inferior left ventricular wall.

open.q: In a right-dominant heart, which artery gives rise to the posterior interventricular artery?

questions.q: Which remnant connects the arch of the aorta to the proximal left pulmonary artery and represents the obliterated fetal ductus arteriosus?
questions.explain: The ligamentum arteriosum is the fibrous remnant of the fetal ductus arteriosus, stretching from the inferior aspect of the aortic arch to the superior aspect of the left pulmonary artery.

open.q: What fibrous cord connects the aortic arch to the left pulmonary artery after closure of the ductus arteriosus?

questions.q: How does bucket-handle movement of lower ribs (approximately ribs 7 to 10) increase the transverse diameter of the thorax?
options: Elevated rib shafts swing their outward-bowed midpoints upward and laterally
The sternum moves down toward the pelvis
questions.explain: Because the middle/lateral aspects of ribs 7 to 10 bow outward and downward, elevating them rotates them like a bucket handle so their lateral arches move outward and upward, widening the transverse thoracic diameter.

open.q: How does bucket-handle motion of the ribs widen the transverse diameter of the thorax?
accept: elevating the curved rib shafts swings their lateral arches outward and upward
lateral rib arcs move outward and upward as the ribs elevate
outward and upward swing of the rib shafts

questions.q: Which lymphoid organ lies predominantly in the anterior/superior mediastinum and is prominent in infants and children before undergoing involution after puberty?
questions.explain: The thymus is a bilobed lymphoid organ located in the anterior and superior mediastinum (retrosternal/anterior to the great vessels and pericardium) where T lymphocytes mature, gradually undergoing fatty involution after puberty.

open.q: Which bilobed lymphoid organ sits in the anterior/superior mediastinum and involutes after puberty?

questions.q: A patient has a tumor or enlarged lymph node in the posterior mediastinum compressing the thoracic duct. Along which side of the body is chylothorax or impaired lymphatic drainage from the lower body most classically associated?
questions.explain: The thoracic duct ascends through the posterior mediastinum and crosses toward the left around T4 to T6 to drain into the left systemic venous junction; injury or obstruction can cause chylothorax (often left-sided or bilateral) and impair lower-body lymph return.

open.q: Toward which side of the thorax does the thoracic duct incline superiorly to drain into the systemic veins?

questions.q: During dissection of a typical rib, the articular facet on its tubercle is identified. Which structure does this facet normally meet?
options: The body of the corresponding thoracic vertebra
The transverse process of the corresponding thoracic vertebra
The spinous process of the vertebra above
The costal cartilage of the rib below
questions.explain: The tubercle of a typical rib has an articular facet that meets the transverse costal facet on the transverse process of the corresponding thoracic vertebra. The head of the rib articulates with vertebral bodies and the intervening disc.

open.q: What does the articular facet on the tubercle of a typical rib articulate with?
accept: transverse process of the corresponding thoracic vertebra
transverse costal facet of the corresponding vertebra

questions.q: A surgeon exposes the internal thoracic artery from the posterior aspect of the anterior chest wall. Which muscle lies posterior to this artery along much of its course?
questions.explain: The internal thoracic artery descends on the inner surface of the anterior thoracic wall, posterior to the costal cartilages and anterior to the transversus thoracis muscle. It terminates around the sixth intercostal space as the superior epigastric and musculophrenic arteries.

open.q: Which muscle lies posterior to the internal thoracic artery on the inner anterior thoracic wall?

questions.q: During breast surgery, the surgeon identifies a loose connective-tissue plane that allows the mammary gland to move over the deep fascia covering pectoralis major. What is this plane called?
questions.explain: The retromammary space is a loose connective-tissue plane between the posterior surface of the breast and the deep pectoral fascia. It permits mobility of the breast over the pectoral region.

open.q: What is the loose connective-tissue plane between the breast and deep pectoral fascia called?

questions.q: A woman with carcinoma in the lateral part of the breast undergoes assessment for regional spread. Which lymph-node group is the most frequent initial destination for lymph from much of the breast?
options: Axillary nodes, especially the pectoral group
questions.explain: Most lymph from the breast, particularly its lateral quadrants, drains to the axillary nodes, especially the anterior (pectoral) group. Medial breast regions also drain to parasternal nodes, and cross-midline drainage can occur.

open.q: Which regional lymph-node basin receives most lymph from the breast, particularly its lateral part?

questions.q: A patient with pleurisy reports sharp pain when the inflamed pleura is stretched during breathing. Which part of the pleura is most directly responsible for well-localized pain?
options: Parietal pleura lining the thoracic wall
questions.explain: The parietal pleura has somatic sensory innervation from intercostal and phrenic nerves and is sensitive to pain. The visceral pleura is supplied by autonomic fibres and is relatively insensitive to ordinary pain, touch and temperature.

open.q: Which pleural layer is sensitive to pain and produces well-localized pleuritic pain?

questions.q: A histological section of lung shows a very thin squamous epithelial cell lining that forms most of the alveolar surface and minimizes the diffusion distance for gases. Which cell type is being observed?
questions.explain: Type I pneumocytes are thin squamous cells covering most of the alveolar surface and form a major part of the blood–air barrier. Type II pneumocytes secrete pulmonary surfactant and can proliferate to replace damaged alveolar epithelial cells.

open.q: Which pneumocyte type forms most of the thin gas-exchanging alveolar surface?

questions.q: A patient has an infarct involving the posterior wall of the right atrium near the opening of the superior vena cava. Which normal pacemaker structure is located in this region?
questions.explain: The sinoatrial node lies subepicardially near the superior end of the crista terminalis at the junction of the superior vena cava and right atrium. It normally initiates the cardiac impulse.

open.q: Which cardiac pacemaker lies near the junction of the superior vena cava and right atrium?

questions.q: In a typical right-dominant coronary circulation, which artery most commonly gives rise to the posterior interventricular artery?
questions.explain: In right-dominant circulation, the posterior interventricular (posterior descending) artery arises from the right coronary artery. Coronary dominance is defined by the artery that gives rise to this vessel; left dominance occurs when it arises from the circumflex artery.

open.q: Which coronary artery usually gives rise to the posterior interventricular artery in right-dominant circulation?

questions.q: A surgeon identifies the greater thoracic splanchnic nerve descending from the thoracic sympathetic trunk. Where do most of its preganglionic sympathetic fibres synapse?
questions.explain: The greater thoracic splanchnic nerve is formed mainly by preganglionic sympathetic fibres from approximately T5–T9 (with variation) and usually synapses in the celiac ganglia. Its postganglionic fibres then distribute to foregut structures.

open.q: In which prevertebral ganglion do most greater thoracic splanchnic nerve fibres synapse?

questions.q: During an operation, the surgeon identifies the opening in the diaphragm transmitting the inferior vena cava. At which vertebral level is this opening usually found?
questions.explain: The caval opening lies in the central tendon of the diaphragm at approximately T8 and transmits the inferior vena cava and terminal branches of the right phrenic nerve. The oesophageal hiatus is at T10 and the aortic hiatus at T12.

open.q: At what vertebral level is the caval opening of the diaphragm located?

questions.q: A patient undergoes repair of a congenital diaphragmatic defect. Which combination correctly lists the major embryological components that contribute to formation of the diaphragm?
options: Septum transversum, pleuroperitoneal membranes, dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus, and muscular ingrowth from the body wall
Neural crest, notochord, and pharyngeal arches
Pleuropericardial membranes and the ventral mesentery of the stomach
Endoderm of the foregut and ectoderm of the thoracic wall
questions.explain: The diaphragm develops from four major components: septum transversum, pleuroperitoneal membranes, dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus, and muscular ingrowth from the lateral body walls. Their incomplete fusion can result in congenital diaphragmatic hernia.

open.q: Name the four major embryological components that form the diaphragm.
accept: septum transversum, pleuroperitoneal membranes, dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus, and body wall musculature
septum transversum pleuroperitoneal membranes dorsal mesentery of oesophagus muscular ingrowth from body wall

questions.q: A developmental abnormality prevents normal formation of the pleuropericardial folds. Which adult structure would be most directly affected by failure of these folds to develop and fuse normally?
options: Fibrous pericardium and separation of the pleural from pericardial cavities
Visceral pleura covering the lungs only
questions.explain: Pleuropericardial folds grow medially and fuse to separate the pericardial cavity from the pleural cavities. They contribute to the fibrous pericardium and the parietal layer of serous pericardium.

open.q: Which cavities are separated by fusion of the pleuropericardial membranes?
accept: pleural cavities from the pericardial cavity

questions.q: A congenital anomaly affects formation of the respiratory diverticulum. From which embryonic structure does this diverticulum normally arise?
questions.explain: The respiratory diverticulum (lung bud) develops as an outgrowth from the ventral wall of the foregut endoderm. Endoderm forms the epithelial lining of the respiratory tract, while surrounding splanchnic mesoderm contributes cartilage, smooth muscle and connective tissue.

open.q: From which part of the embryonic gut does the respiratory diverticulum arise?

questions.q: A medical student is asked to arrange the major stages of lung development in chronological order. Which sequence is correct?
questions.explain: The major stages of lung development proceed through the pseudoglandular, canalicular, terminal sac (saccular), and alveolar periods. These stages overlap in time, and alveolar maturation continues after birth.

open.q: List the four major periods of lung development in chronological order.

questions.q: A penetrating injury just posterior to the sternum at the level of the second intercostal space damages a structure in the superior mediastinum. Which vessel lies immediately posterior to the manubrium and anterior to the branches of the aortic arch?
questions.explain: The left brachiocephalic vein crosses obliquely behind the manubrium, anterior to the branches of the aortic arch, to join the right brachiocephalic vein and form the superior vena cava.

open.q: Name the structure or anatomical relationship tested in this clinical scenario.

questions.q: A central lung tumour obstructs the right main bronchus. Compared with the left main bronchus, which anatomical feature predisposes the right main bronchus to aspiration of foreign bodies?
options: It is wider, shorter and more vertical
It is narrower, longer and more horizontal
It passes beneath the aortic arch
questions.explain: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left, making aspirated objects more likely to enter it.

open.q: Name the structure or anatomical relationship tested in this clinical scenario.
accept: it is wider, shorter and more vertical

questions.q: During cardiac surgery, the surgeon opens the pericardial cavity posterior to the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk. Which space is entered?
questions.explain: The transverse pericardial sinus lies posterior to the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk and anterior to the superior vena cava and atria.

open.q: Name the structure or anatomical relationship tested in this clinical scenario.

questions.q: A patient has a penetrating wound at the eighth intercostal space near the midaxillary line. To avoid the main intercostal neurovascular bundle, where should a chest tube be introduced relative to the rib?
options: Immediately superior to the upper border of the rib below
Immediately inferior to the lower border of the rib above
Through the centre of the intercostal space
questions.explain: The main intercostal vein, artery and nerve run in the costal groove along the inferior border of the rib above. A tube is passed just superior to the upper border of the rib below.

open.q: Name the structure or anatomical relationship tested in this clinical scenario.
accept: immediately superior to the upper border of the rib below

questions.q: A patient with an enlarged left atrium develops dysphagia. Which structure is compressed by the enlarged chamber?
questions.explain: The oesophagus lies immediately posterior to the left atrium, so marked left atrial enlargement may compress it and cause dysphagia.

open.q: Name the structure or anatomical relationship tested in this clinical scenario.

questions.q: A patient with a small pleural effusion is examined while sitting upright. In which pleural recess does fluid most commonly collect initially?
questions.explain: The costodiaphragmatic recess is the largest pleural recess and is the dependent region where pleural fluid commonly accumulates in an upright patient.

open.q: A patient with a small pleural effusion is examined while sitting upright. In which pleural recess does fluid most commonly collect initially?

questions.q: A foreign body is aspirated while a child is playing. Which anatomical feature makes the right main bronchus a more frequent site of lodgement than the left?
options: It is wider, shorter and more vertical
It is narrower, longer and more horizontal
It arises at a higher level than the trachea
questions.explain: The right main bronchus is typically wider, shorter and more vertical than the left, making it a more direct continuation of the trachea.

open.q: A foreign body is aspirated while a child is playing. Which anatomical feature makes the right main bronchus a more frequent site of lodgement than the left?

questions.q: During thoracic surgery, the thoracic duct is identified in the posterior mediastinum. At which vertebral level does it usually cross from right to left behind the oesophagus?
questions.explain: The thoracic duct commonly ascends on the right side of the vertebral column and crosses to the left around T5, posterior to the oesophagus. Anatomical variation occurs.

open.q: During thoracic surgery, the thoracic duct is identified in the posterior mediastinum. At which vertebral level does it usually cross from right to left behind the oesophagus?

questions.q: A patient has obstruction of the azygos vein near its termination. Which major venous channel normally receives the azygos arch?
questions.explain: The azygos vein ascends on the right side of the vertebral column, arches over the root of the right lung and drains into the superior vena cava.

open.q: A patient has obstruction of the azygos vein near its termination. Which major venous channel normally receives the azygos arch?

questions.q: During cardiac surgery, a clamp is passed through the transverse pericardial sinus. Which structures form its anterior and posterior boundaries?
options: Ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk anteriorly; superior vena cava and left atrium posteriorly
Superior vena cava anteriorly; right ventricle posteriorly
Pulmonary veins anteriorly; inferior vena cava posteriorly
questions.explain: The transverse pericardial sinus lies posterior to the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk and anterior to the superior vena cava and upper part of the left atrium.

open.q: During cardiac surgery, a clamp is passed through the transverse pericardial sinus. Which structures form its anterior and posterior boundaries?
accept: Aorta and pulmonary trunk anteriorly; SVC and left atrium posteriorly

questions.q: A patient has a penetrating wound through the diaphragm at the level of T10. Which structure is most likely to be injured at this opening?
questions.explain: The oesophageal hiatus is at approximately T10 and transmits the oesophagus and vagal trunks. The caval opening is at T8 and the aortic hiatus at T12.

open.q: A patient has a penetrating wound through the diaphragm at the level of T10. Which structure is most likely to be injured at this opening?

questions.q: A tumour in the thorax causes hoarseness by affecting a nerve that loops under the aortic arch. Which nerve is involved?
questions.explain: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the arch of the aorta near the ligamentum arteriosum and ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove. Injury may produce hoarseness.

open.q: A tumour in the thorax causes hoarseness by affecting a nerve that loops under the aortic arch. Which nerve is involved?

questions.q: A coronary angiogram shows that the posterior interventricular artery arises from the right coronary artery. What is this coronary circulation pattern called?
questions.explain: Coronary dominance is defined by the origin of the posterior interventricular artery. Its origin from the right coronary artery indicates right dominance.

open.q: A coronary angiogram shows that the posterior interventricular artery arises from the right coronary artery. What is this coronary circulation pattern called?

questions.q: A surgeon plans a segmental resection for a localised bronchiectatic lesion. Which anatomical feature makes an individual bronchopulmonary segment suitable for removal?
options: It is supplied by a segmental bronchus and a corresponding branch of the pulmonary artery
It shares one common segmental bronchus with every adjacent segment
Its veins run centrally alongside the segmental bronchus
It is separated from neighbouring segments by a complete pleural cavity
questions.explain: Each bronchopulmonary segment is a surgically resectable unit supplied by a segmental (tertiary) bronchus and a segmental branch of the pulmonary artery. Pulmonary veins usually run in intersegmental planes.

open.q: What bronchial and arterial structures supply an individual bronchopulmonary segment?
accept: A segmental bronchus and a corresponding segmental branch of the pulmonary artery

questions.q: A mass in the middle mediastinum compresses a structure that carries deoxygenated blood from the upper body to the right atrium. Which vessel is affected?
questions.explain: The superior vena cava lies in the superior and middle mediastinal region and returns venous blood from the head, neck, upper limbs and thoracic wall to the right atrium.

open.q: Which large vein returns blood from the head, neck and upper limbs to the right atrium?
